title: Proxy connection reuse & TLS handshake telemetry — field notes
content:
Summary:
This is a working log of short experiments exploring how connection reuse, TLS handshake behavior, and proxy connection pooling interact with streaming LLM responses (HTTP/1.1 chunking and HTTP/2 gRPC). The goal: explain several odd latency tail behaviors we've seen in staging and propose mitigations for our hosted API path (Envoy sidecar + external ingress proxy).

Top-level findings (quick):
- TLS handshake on new TCP connections adds a consistent ~8–12ms median overhead to first-response for short responses; p95 impact can spike to 25–40ms when CPU is contended on the proxy host.
- Connection reuse (keepalives) eliminates the TLS cost but exposes occasional head-of-line stalls when the proxy's connection pool is saturated and requests queue behind a long-running streaming response (gRPC bidi / HTTP chunk streaming).
- Envoy config knobs (max-requests-per-connection, connection-buffer-limit) have measurable tradeoffs: aggressive reuse reduces median but increases jitter under high-concurrency; aggressive connection turnover lowers jitter but increases median.
- Small-chunk streaming (flush every 64B–256B) increases server CPU/syscall overhead and amplifies latency variance through proxies that perform per-chunk buffering/reassembly (some L7 proxies do this).

Context and why this matters:
- Product teams rely on sub-50ms p50 for short completions (search reranking, metadata-only requests). We observed inexplicable p95 spikes up to 200ms in hosted API over the last month. Many of those spikes correlate with bursts of new client connections (e.g., ephemeral mobile clients).
- Hypothesis: combination of (a) TLS handshake on new TCP connections, (b) proxy connection pooling limits, and (c) per-chunk handling in the proxy creates a ladder of delays.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Targets: model-serving pods (gniazdo-infer-rt) behind an Envoy sidecar, and fronted by a managed ingress (edge-proxy) — experiments vary sidecar vs direct, and TLS termination point (edge vs pod).
- Variables: TLS termination location (edge TLS vs mTLS to sidecar), connection reuse policy (keepalive timeouts, max requests/conn), client concurrency profile (bursts vs steady), streaming chunk size (1KB, 256B, 64B), proxy implementation (Envoy 1.28, nginx-ingress controller, haproxy), HTTP versions (HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 gRPC streaming).
- Metrics collected: first-byte latency, end-to-end p50/p95/p99, TLS handshake durations (where visible), connection churn, active connection counts on proxy, proxy CPU, syscall rates (send/recv), and per-chunk times (when instrumented).

Representative commands / harness:
- load generator: k6 + python harness to open X concurrent clients with new connection probability P_new and stream chunk size S. Example k6 scenario snippet used locally (pseudo):
  - open_connection(new_prob=P_new) -> send request -> stream S bytes per chunk until complete -> close or keepalive based on policy
- on-proxy socket stats: ss -tanp | grep envoy  (to track TIME_WAIT / ESTAB churn)
- Envoy admin stats scraping: /stats?filter=cluster.cluster_name.* and server.concurrency counters

Selected raw observations (abridged):
- Baseline (no TLS, direct pod): p50 22ms, p95 35ms for short responses (250–600B). CPU ~12% on pod.
- Edge TLS termination (edge->envoy->pod plain): p50 32ms, p95 70ms. Observed TLS handshakes per second spike when client churn high; median TLS handshake measured ~9ms.
- mTLS (edge TLS + mTLS to sidecar, reusing connections): p50 24ms, p95 90ms -- note: median recovered but p95 worsened because sidecar connection queueing introduced 50–100ms stalls when sidecar had >200 active downstream requests per upstream connection.
- Envoy with max_requests_per_connection=0 (unlimited): median 20–25ms; p99 occasionally 300–600ms under bursty arrivals due to head-of-line blocking on long-lived streaming responses.
- Envoy with max_requests_per_connection=100: p50 30ms, p95 80ms — slightly higher medians but lower rare tails, because connections are recycled sooner reducing single-connection queuing.

Notes on chunking/backpressure behavior:
- When streaming with very small writes (64B), per-chunk syscall rate skyrockets on both client and proxy; proxy CPU jumps ~2.3x. Some proxies (older nginx versions) buffer small writes until a threshold, effectively coalescing but adding ~5–20ms per-chunk delay. Envoy tends to forward chunks promptly but with per-chunk context switches that add jitter.
- Backpressure from slow downstream (client) can cause upstream request queuing inside the proxy if its concurrency model ties requests to connections. In our setup, when multiple clients re-used the same backend connection, a slow streaming client could block others.

Behavior differences: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 (gRPC)
- HTTP/2 multiplexing avoids head-of-line on connection-level if the proxy implements true multiplexing. However we observed two practical issues: (1) some proxies perform flow-control based on connection-level windowing and a single large stream can reduce per-stream window availability leading to stalls; (2) proxies that terminate HTTP/2 and proxy to backends over HTTP/1.1 reintroduce H1 per-connection blocking.
- gRPC with many small messages: better tail in ideal multiplexing proxy, worse when the proxy has conservative per-stream flow control settings.

Proxy-specific oddities found: 
- Envoy sidecars on nodes with bursty workloads show TLS rekey operations (rotation) happening in the middle of bursts — we need to verify if our cert rotation timing interacts badly with connection reuse lifetimes.
- Some managed external edge proxies do per-request ACL checks that add 2–6ms external lookup latency which compounds with TLS.

Practical mitigations tested (and quick results):
- Encourage connection reuse from clients (keepalive, HTTP/2) for workloads dominated by short completions — reduces median notably. But combine with max_requests_per_connection to avoid pathological queuing.
- Configure Envoy: set max_requests_per_connection ~ 50–200, idle_keepalive 60s, upstream stream_idle_timeout tuned for longer-lived streaming requests. This reduced p99 in our tests from ~400ms -> ~120ms in bursty scenarios.
- Adjust chunking on server-side: coalesce small writes at server SDK layer into ~512B–1KB frames when possible — best throughput/latency tradeoff for our runtime.
- Monitor TLS handshakes per-second on ingress (add Prometheus metric) and add alerting (threshold: > 10% new connections/sec relative to total RPS) — indicates mobile/ephemeral client surge where connection pooling is ineffective.
- For extreme low-latency short RPCs, consider a mixed path: allow occasional plaintext internal connections over private VPC for dedicated customers to avoid TLS cost, documented and gated by policy.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Are cert rotation windows causing transient TLS renegotiation? Add detailed tracing at TLS layer (libssl metrics) to confirm.
- We need a microbenchmark of client-side ephemeral library (SDK) behavior on iOS/Android to quantify new-conn probability under app cold starts.
- Validate edge-managed proxies' per-chunk buffering behavior with packet captures — some signs of reassembly happening at the edge rather than at sidecar.
- Re-run same matrix with server CPU pinned and with QAT (TLS offload) enabled on edge to confirm interaction between CPU contention and handshake latency.

Appendix — quick config snippets (rough):
- envoy cluster config excerpt we used: (pseudo)
  cluster: 
    max_requests_per_connection: 100
    connect_timeout: 250ms
    per_connection_buffer_limit_bytes: 1048576

- server SDK coalescing: accumulate up to 1KB or 10ms before flushing chunk (configurable)

Concluding note:
This doc is not complete — it's a set of working notes and a hypothesis-driven checklist. Next steps: automate the matrix (k6 + infra provisioning via terratest), add TLS handshake metric to the ingress dashboards, and draft recommended Envoy defaults for hosted API (balance median vs tail).

If you're poking this: leave TODO pointers inline or add results from mobile SDK runs in a new section.

-- Priya
